items.title: Sprinting and marathon running use chemically different fuels
items.claim: Aerobic respiration of one glucose produces about 30-32 ATP. Anaerobic glycolysis produces only 2 ATP. Yet sprinters rely on the anaerobic path. Why use a pathway that wastes 94% of glucose's chemical energy?

options.text: It's faster — sprint muscle can produce ATP via glycolysis ~100x faster per second than oxidative phosphorylation can. Power output wins over efficiency in short bursts

items.reveal:
Aerobic respiration is the efficient long path: glycolysis (cytoplasm) -> pyruvate -> Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) -> oxidative phosphorylation -> ~30-32 ATP per glucose, with CO2 and water as byproducts.

Anaerobic glycolysis stops at pyruvate, converts it to lactate (regenerating the NAD+ glycolysis needs), and quits. Yield: 2 ATP per glucose. But it runs without oxygen and at ~100x the rate of mitochondrial ATP synthesis.

Sprint events (100m, weightlifting): mostly anaerobic. Lactate builds up. Burns. The 'oxygen debt' you owe after sprinting is the cost of clearing the lactate and replenishing phosphocreatine.

Endurance events (marathon, cycling): mostly aerobic, fuelled by glucose at first, then fat. Fat yields ~106 ATP per palmitate molecule but is metabolised slowly — fine for steady output.

Yeasts do alcoholic fermentation (pyruvate -> ethanol + CO2) instead of lactate fermentation. Same logic: regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolysis running when oxygen runs low.
items.why: Efficiency seems obviously best. For peak power, throughput beats efficiency every time — which is why sprinters look chemically different from marathoners during a race.

items.title: Bees die when they sting — and this makes evolutionary sense
items.claim: A worker bee that stings a mammal disembowels itself and dies. Sterile, suicidal workers shouldn't exist if natural selection works at the individual level. They do exist, abundantly.
items.prompt: How does evolution favour individuals that don't reproduce?

options.text: Natural selection doesn't really work for social insects

Hamilton's rule: a gene for altruism spreads if rB is greater than C (relatedness times benefit exceeds cost); worker bees share 75 percent of their genes with sisters due to haplodiploidy, so helping the queen reproduce passes on their own genes effectively
Queen bees control workers chemically against their interests

items.reveal:
W. D. Hamilton wrote the equation rB greater than C: a gene for helping behaviour spreads if the relatedness (r) times the benefit to the recipient (B) exceeds the cost to the actor (C).

In haplodiploid Hymenoptera (bees, ants, wasps), females are diploid (from a diploid mother and a haploid father), males are haploid (unfertilised eggs). A worker shares 50 percent of her genes with her own offspring (if she had any), but 75 percent with her full sisters — because their shared father is haploid and gave them ALL his genes.

So a worker's gene-propagation interest is best served by helping her mother (the queen) make more sisters. Sterility is rational from the gene's perspective.

Hamilton's work, building on J. B. S. Haldane's quip 'I would lay down my life for two brothers or eight cousins', founded sociobiology.
items.why: Selection is taught as acting on individuals. The gene's-eye view explains altruism, sociality and self-sacrifice — phenomena that the individual-level view can't easily handle.

items.title: Mosses spend most of their lives haploid — like permanent eggs
items.claim: Animals are diploid (two copies of each chromosome) and reduce to haploid (one copy) only briefly in sperm and eggs. Mosses live mostly as haploid (gametophyte) plants. The diploid sporophyte is a tiny stalk that grows from the haploid plant, makes spores, and dies.
items.prompt: What does alternation of generations mean?

options.text: Plants alternate between adult and juvenile forms

The life cycle alternates between a multicellular haploid stage (gametophyte) and a multicellular diploid stage (sporophyte); both are 'organisms' in their own right, unlike animals where only the diploid stage is recognisable as an individual
Genes alternate between being expressed and silent
Generations alternate between male and female

items.reveal:
The full plant life cycle: gametes (haploid, n) fuse to make a zygote (diploid, 2n) -> sporophyte (2n) develops -> meiosis -> spores (n) -> spores germinate into gametophytes (n) -> gametophytes make gametes (n) -> cycle repeats.

Mosses: gametophyte dominant (the leafy green plant). Sporophyte is the stalk with a capsule, attached to and dependent on the gametophyte.

Ferns: sporophyte dominant (the leafy plant). Gametophyte is a tiny independent heart-shaped prothallus, easy to miss.

Flowering plants: sporophyte hugely dominant (the tree, the grass). Gametophyte is microscopic — pollen grains (male, 3 cells) and embryo sacs inside ovules (female, 7-8 cells). Both are dependent on the sporophyte parent.

Evolutionary trend: gametophytes have become progressively smaller, more dependent, more protected. Flowering plants reduce them to barely-cellular structures.

In animals, only the diploid stage is multicellular; gametes are single cells. No alternation in the plant sense.
items.why: The 'plant' you see in your garden is one of two organisms in a single life cycle. The other organism — the gametophyte — has been reduced and hidden in flowering plants, but it's still there inside every pollen grain.
